items.why: The contrast is recoverable, but the broad negative question is unnatural and underspecified.
Ambiguous pronouns make it unclear whether the question targets the speaker or the man of God.
The closing summary clearly distinguishes the collective victors from Jonathan, who killed only one descendant.
The officer is identifiable, but this duplicates the more explicit officer-trampling item.
The old prophet’s request and subsequent mounting are explicit, while his sons only saddle the donkey.
The passage clearly distinguishes the first three-party covenant from the later two-party covenant.
Jotham’s succession is the explicit event following Uzziah’s burial.
The passage directly states that Uzziah was eager to leave because the Lord had afflicted him.
The intended sequence is clear, but the wording about following the capture is awkward.
Their decision to surrender at the Aramean camp is explicit and contrasts with the rejected city option.
The textual sequence supports Sibbekai, though asking who kills “first” is somewhat mechanical.
“The news” is a vague, incomplete answer that merely repeats the reporting language.
Jeroboam’s direct command clearly targets the man of God, not himself.
Uzziah enters first and is explicitly the person Azariah and the priests follow.
The quoted plan cleanly contrasts eating one child today with the other tomorrow.
Zechariah is explicitly identified as Uzziah’s instructor in the fear of God.
Elisha’s reply to the officer’s doubt is clearly separated from his earlier price prophecy.
The man of God explicitly grounds his refusal in the Lord’s command.
Talking until daylight is the last stated action before Paul leaves.
Mobilizing the army clearly precedes marching and laying siege, though the task is simple sequencing.
Jehoiada explicitly gives the weapons; David is only their former owner.
The speaker explicitly orders the accusers to present their case to the addressee.
The purpose is clear, but “take Amaziah’s son” is less natural than naming Uzziah.
The passage explicitly places the 307,500 men under the 2,600 family leaders’ command.
The traveling man of God is unambiguously the person met and killed by the lion.
The officer placed at the gate is explicitly trampled there, cleanly excluding the king.
The passage specifically assigns the two off-duty companies to guard the temple for the king.
The letter heading plainly identifies Claudius Lysias as writer and Felix as recipient.
Abishai’s victim is explicitly the Philistine threatening David, making the contrast decisive.
After acknowledging wrongdoing, the men explicitly decide to report immediately to the palace.
Paul’s quoted words explicitly identify the young man as having information for the commander.
The messengers’ return and report occur immediately before the camp is plundered.
The final clause clearly attributes the love of soil to Uzziah rather than his workers.
The speaker explicitly says her own son was cooked and eaten before the other child was hidden.
The man of God explicitly intercedes after the king asks him to pray.
The passage supplies a complete, explicit list of the three peoples God helped Uzziah against.
The prophet first brings the body to his city and only afterward places it in his tomb.
Joash is explicitly hidden with his nurse for six years, while Ahaziah is already dead.
The passage directly attributes the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death at the palace.
The two centurions are directly addressed and ordered to prepare the listed forces.
The Arameans explicitly believe the hired Hittite and Egyptian kings are coming to attack.
The king is the sender whom Elisha calls a murderer; the messenger is the person being sent.
“According to the claim” appropriately targets the old prophet’s assertion about the man of God.
The passage explicitly links Paul’s prolonged speaking to his intention to leave the next day.
The contrast indicates the non-cavalry soldiers return, though “soldiers” can broadly include cavalry.
The seven sons are unmistakably the beaten group who flee naked and bleeding.
The intended answer is clear, but “on the items’ arrival” is an awkward and inferred formulation.
The conspirators explicitly ask the council to petition the commander to bring Paul.
The sorcery practitioners explicitly burn the scrolls immediately after bringing them together.
The explicit sword order targets anyone following Athaliah, while her own execution is described separately.
Hearing the guards’ and people’s noise explicitly prompts Athaliah to go to the crowd.
The commander’s consent is an explicit trigger, but the broad verb “act” leaves some interpretive room.
The warning is directly addressed to the man of God from Judah, not the old prophet.
The prophecy explicitly names Josiah as the person who will sacrifice the high-place priests.
